passages.happening:
‘About that time there was a great outcry from the people and their wives against their fellow Jews’ (verse 1).

Three groups speak, each a step deeper into poverty. Some say, “We and our sons and daughters are numerous. We must get grain in order to eat and stay alive” (verse 2). Others say, “We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our homes to get grain during the famine” (verse 3). Still others say that they have borrowed money ‘to pay the king’s tax on our fields and vineyards’ (verse 4).

And the worst: ‘yet we are subjecting our sons and daughters to slavery. Some of our daughters are already enslaved, but we are powerless to redeem them because our fields and vineyards belong to others’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 4 ended with the community armed against enemies outside the walls. Chapter 5 turns to a threat from inside, in some ways a worse one. Some members of the community were growing rich by driving others into poverty and bondage.

Judah under Persian rule was a small farming province. The empire collected tribute from every province, often in silver, and a small farmer who had to pay in silver in a bad year had little choice but to borrow. There was a famine, and the builders' time on the wall may have kept men from their fields. The result was a pattern familiar across the ancient world: poor farmers pledged their land, and at last their children, to wealthy lenders.

The word for outcry, tseaqah, is the word for the cry of the oppressed that reaches God's ears, as Israel's cry did in Egypt. A first hearer would know what kind of cry this was.

The law of Moses allowed lending, but it forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite. It allowed a poor man to sell his labor to pay a debt, but it required that he be treated as a hired worker and not as a slave, and that he be set free in the year of release. Those protections had broken down. And the cry is against fellow Jews: brothers selling brothers.
passages.later: The law was plain: ‘If you lend money to one of My people among you who is poor, you must not act as a creditor to him; you are not to charge him interest’ (Exodus 22:25). And again: ‘Do not take any interest or profit from him, but fear your God, that your countryman may live among you’ (Leviticus 25:36).
passages.hard:
Why does the Bible allow people to sell their children into servitude at all?

The chapter does not approve of what is happening. It presents the bondage of children as a crisis that makes Nehemiah angry and that he works to end. Still, readers rightly ask why the law of Moses allowed debt service in the first place.

In the ancient Near East, when a family fell into debt with no land or goods left, selling labor was often the only alternative to starving. The law of Moses did not invent the practice; it regulated it. It required that an Israelite in debt service be treated as a hired worker and not as a slave, it limited the term, and it commanded release with provisions. It also forbade interest to the poor, which was meant to keep families from falling into such debt at all.

Some interpreters see these laws as God meeting a harsh economy where it was and restraining its worst abuses, while pointing toward a fuller justice. Others stress that the laws, faithfully kept, would have made lasting poverty nearly impossible. On either reading, this chapter shows how quickly the protections were ignored when they cost the wealthy something, and how the prophets and reformers treated that neglect as a sin against God.

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The cry came from inside the community, against its own leaders. Ask whose outcry you might be too comfortable to hear. And ask whether anything you profit from is paid for by someone else's debt.

passages.happening:
‘When I heard their outcry and these complaints, I became extremely angry’ (verse 6). After serious thought he rebukes the nobles and officials: “You are exacting usury from your own brothers!” (verse 7). He calls a large assembly. “We have done our best to buy back our Jewish brothers who were sold to foreigners, but now you are selling your own brothers, that they may be sold back to us!” (verse 8). They are silent, for they can find nothing to say.

“What you are doing is not right. Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God to avoid the reproach of our foreign enemies?” (verse 9). Nehemiah includes himself: he and his brothers and servants have been lending money and grain too. “Please, let us stop this usury” (verse 10). He asks them to give back the fields, vineyards, olive groves and houses at once, with the interest they have been charging (verse 11).

“We will restore it,” they replied, and they swear an oath before the priests (verse 12). Nehemiah shakes out the fold of his robe as a sign: may God shake out of his house anyone who breaks this promise. The whole assembly says amen and praises the LORD. ‘And the people did as they had promised’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Nehemiah's anger is not a loss of control. He thinks before he acts, and then he acts in public, before the whole assembly, so that the promise will be public too.

His appeal is not to a new ideal but to the covenant they already had, and to the fear of God, the reverent awe that shapes how a person lives. He also names the shame before their enemies. A community that sells its own brothers gives its neighbors a reason to mock its God.

The percentage of verse 11, literally the hundredth part, is taken by many interpreters as interest of one percent a month, though its exact meaning is uncertain.

The shaking of the robe is a public sign-act. A garment gathered at the waist could serve as a pocket; Nehemiah empties it out and pronounces a curse on anyone who breaks the oath. The assembly's amen binds them to it. And the chapter adds, simply, that they kept it.
passages.later:
Paul made the same kind of sign in Corinth when he turned from those who opposed him: ‘he shook out his garments’ (Acts 18:6).

The law of release stands behind the whole scene: ‘If a fellow Hebrew, a man or a woman, is sold to you and serves you six years, then in the seventh year you must set him free’ (Deuteronomy 15:12).
passages.asks: Nehemiah asked them to stop, and counted himself among those who must change. Ask where you need to stop something that is legal but not right. And ask whether you can confront wrong without excusing yourself.

passages.t: A governor who did not take his allowance
passages.happening:
Nehemiah looks back over his years as governor. ‘Furthermore, from the day King Artaxerxes appointed me to be their governor in the land of Judah, from his twentieth year until his thirty-second year (twelve years total), neither I nor my brothers ate the food allotted to the governor’ (verse 14).

‘The governors before me had heavily burdened the people, taking from them bread and wine plus forty shekels of silver. Their servants also oppressed the people, but I did not do this because of my fear of God’ (verse 15). He gave himself to the work on the wall and acquired no land (verse 16). A hundred and fifty Jews and officials ate at his table, besides guests from the nations around, and he provided for them without demanding the governor's food allowance, ‘because the burden on the people was so heavy’ (verse 18).

The chapter ends with a prayer: ‘Remember me favorably, O my God, for all that I have done for this people’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The twentieth to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes I is about 445 to 433 BC. This part of the chapter is written later, looking back over those twelve years.

A governor in the Persian period was expected to keep a great table for officials and visitors, at great expense, and the earlier governors had laid the cost on the people. Nehemiah paid it himself. He uses the same reason he gave the nobles: the fear of God.

The closing prayer is the first of several in which Nehemiah asks God to remember him. It is not a claim to have earned salvation. It is a request that God take note of faithfulness done at personal cost. For this book, a rebuilt city with an unjust economy is not a restored city, and a leader who takes from the poor is not fit to lead them.
passages.later: The same prayer comes back at the end of the book: ‘Remember me, O my God, with favor’ (Nehemiah 13:31). And the people's later pledge returns to the law of release: ‘Every seventh year we will let the fields lie fallow, and will cancel every debt’ (Nehemiah 10:31), as Deuteronomy commanded (Deuteronomy 15:1-2).
passages.asks: Nehemiah could have taken what was his by right, and he did not, because the people's burden was heavy. Ask what rights you hold that weigh on others. And ask what it would mean for you to carry a cost so that someone else does not have to.
